# The Present Picker: full gift-idea bank

> Complete text of the gift bank behind thepresentpicker.com: 255 gift ideas, each checked by a person.
> No brands, no stores, no exact prices, only budget bands. The picker on the homepage and the
> Present Picker MCP tools draw on this same bank. Generated 2026-10-27 from the bank source.
> Page sections added 2026-11-06: the thirty-five sitemap pages that had no section in this file
> now have one (see the end of this file), so all sixty-one sitemap pages have a section here.
> Page sections added 2026-11-06 (wave 3): the six wave-3 sitemap pages that had no section in this file
> now have one (see the end of this file), so all sixty-seven sitemap pages have a section here.
> Page sections added 2026-11-06 (wave 4): the two wave-4 sitemap pages that had no section in this file
> now have one (see the end of this file), so all sixty-nine sitemap pages have a section here.

## Site summary

- The Present Picker (https://thepresentpicker.com/) is a free gift finder. Pick the person, and it returns five gift ideas matched to what they are into and your budget.
- Your budget is a hard filter. Your interests score each idea. Same answers, same five picks, every time.
- Every idea is a type of gift, never a link to a shop. Search the name anywhere you like.
- Budget bands: Under $25 / $25 to $50 / $50 to $100 / Over $100.

## Question pages

Pages that each answer one gift question in full, on the page, with the picker's real top picks for that ask. Same bank, same rules: budget is a hard filter, no brands. Most picks carry a plain price-check link to a shopping search; the site earns nothing from it.

### Gifts for Grandma Who Has Everything (https://thepresentpicker.com/gift-for-grandma-who-has-everything)

She says she has everything. She is almost right.
When someone has everything, the gift has to earn its place. The picks below get used up, get used every day, or hold the family close. Nothing here gathers dust on a shelf.
The book everyone will be discussing in January.
Ask printed on the page: These are the picker's real top picks for this ask: a grandparent, sentimental, any budget, from 255 checked ideas.
Picks on the page (8, in page order): Under $25: The year's most talked-about hardcover novel; Soy candle trio, seasonal scents; Heirloom seed collection. $25 to $50: Handmade ceramic mugs, set of two; Custom star-map print of a meaningful date. $50 to $100: Weighted blanket, 15 lb; Chunky knit throw blanket. $100+: Digital photo frame with wifi.

Common questions:
Q: What can I get my grandma who has everything?
A: Give her something that does not add clutter: a gift that gets used up, an upgrade to something she uses daily, or a keepsake that holds the family. The photo frame the family can update and the star-map print both work because they carry people she loves, not more stuff.
Q: What if my grandma says she wants nothing?
A: Believe the feeling, not the words. She means no clutter and no fuss. A small, warm gift still lands: the candle trio, a good novel, or seeds for spring all say you thought of her without filling a shelf.
Q: Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
A: Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link, so it has exactly one job: good ideas.

Q: How much should I spend on a dad who wants nothing?
A: Less than you think. Most of these picks sit between $25 and $50. With this dad, quality beats size: one tool he will use for years beats a big box he has to store.

### White Elephant Gifts That Are Actually Good (https://thepresentpicker.com/white-elephant-gifts)

Funny is easy. Funny and worth stealing is the game.
A good white elephant gift gets fought over. A bad one gets re-gifted to the same party next year. Every pick below stays useful after the laugh fades.
Three bottles with the heat levels labeled and tasting notes on the box.

Common questions:
Q: What makes a white elephant gift actually good?
A: Two things: it makes the room laugh, and the winner is glad to keep it. Aim for funny plus useful. Pure gag gifts die by January; the hot sauce trio and the harmonica get used all year.
Q: How much do people spend on white elephant gifts?
A: Most parties set the limit at $20 or $25. Some go to $50 for a big-splash round. Every pick on this page sits inside one of those two bands.

### Gifts for a Coworker You Barely Know (https://thepresentpicker.com/gifts-for-a-coworker-you-barely-know)

Safe beats clever when you just met them.
The barely-know-them coworker is a narrow target: kind, useful, and not one bit personal. Every pick below stays under $25, works for almost anyone, and asks nothing about their size, their taste, or their life outside work.
Slow weekend coffee with no machine on the counter.

Common questions:
Q: What do you get a coworker you barely know?
A: Something useful that is not personal: a better cable, a book light, a coffee upgrade. It should work even if you know nothing about them but their job. Every pick on this page passes that test and stays under $25.
Q: What should you not give a coworker you barely know?
A: Anything romantic, scented, sized, or jokey about them. Skip gifts that comment on their habits, too. If it could be read as a message, it is the wrong gift.
Q: How much should you spend on a coworker gift?
A: Under $25 is the safe office band. It reads as generous without asking anyone to match you back. All eight picks on this page sit inside it.

Common questions:
Q: What do you buy someone who is hard to buy for?

Q: Are gift cards okay for someone hard to buy for?
A: As a last resort, yes, but a card says you gave up. One specific idea from their set above, even a small one, lands warmer. If you do give a card, pair it with one small real thing.

A: The fast charging cable set, the phone stand with a charging dock, or the travel adapter. All three sit under $25 on this page, and all three get used the week they arrive.

Picks on the page (8, in page order): Over $100: Balance bike; Beginner kids' telescope; Wooden play kitchen; Kids' tablet with parental controls; Wooden play food and market stall set; Boxed illustrated encyclopedia set for kids; Reading nook tent with cushion set; Real wood percussion set for kids.

Common questions:
Q: What is a good gift for a kid over $100?
A: A big gift that fits the stage they are in right now: a balance bike for the kid learning to ride, a telescope for the kid who looks up, a play kitchen for the kid who helps with dinner. At this price, the match matters more than the size.
Q: Is it worth spending over $100 on a kid gift?
A: Only when the gift will be used for months or years, not days. Every pick on this page is built to last past the holiday: solid wood, sturdy frames, and sets that grow with the kid. If the use would be short, the $50 to $100 page, linked above, is the safer spend.
Q: How do I know they will not outgrow it fast?
A: Look for the grow-with-them signs in the buying notes on each card: an adjustable seat, room to add pieces, a set that starts simple and gets harder. Those are the gifts that stay in use longest.
Q: Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
A: Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link, so it has exactly one job: good ideas.

Two hours with a roaster: pour-over, espresso, and a bag to take home.

Why this fits: They come back Monday with a skill the whole office tastes.

Look for: a hands-on class where everyone brews, not a lecture with samples. Avoid: voucher dates that expire within a month of the gift.

Tip: Book a Saturday morning slot so nobody rushes. The take-home bag bridges the wait until the first class.

For: coworker, friend, partner, other. Budget: $100+. Interests: cooking. Styles: experience.

### Instant print camera with a starter film pack

Point, shoot, and a real photo prints in your hand a minute later.

Why this fits: A photo you can pin up beats a hundred sitting in a phone.

Look for: a selfie mirror by the lens and film that is easy to find locally. Avoid: models whose film costs more than a dollar a shot.

Tip: The starter pack goes fast at the first party; add one spare pack. Shade fresh prints from sunlight for the first minute.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: tech. Styles: fun.

### LED strip light kit for a bedroom

A peel-and-stick light run that turns a plain room into their place.

Why this fits: Teenagers spend their lives in that room; this makes it theirs.

Look for: a kit that cuts to length at marked points and a remote with a dimmer. Avoid: strips with no spare adhesive clips; corners peel first.

Tip: Measure the wall run before ordering. A strip behind the headboard or desk edge glows softer than one facing the room.

For: kid. Budget: $25-$50. Interests: tech, cozy. Styles: fun.

### Build-your-own mechanical clock kit

Gears, a pendulum, and a frame that become a clock that really ticks.

Why this fits: Finishing it teaches more mechanics than a term of diagrams.

Look for: wooden gears cut cleanly enough to mesh without force and a weight or spring drive. Avoid: kits that need glue at every joint to hold.

Tip: Build it on a tray so small gears stay found. An hour a weekend is the right pace; rushing the escapement is where kits fail.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: science. Styles: practical, fun.

### Complete skateboard with helmet and pads

An assembled board rated for a teenager, plus the gear that makes parents say yes.

Why this fits: It is the rare gift that gets them outside the same afternoon.

Look for: a deck at least eight inches wide and pads sized for teens, not small children. Avoid: toy-store boards with plastic trucks; they crack under real weight.

Tip: First session on smooth empty pavement, helmet on before the first push. Tighten the wheel nuts once after week one.

For: kid. Budget: $25-$50. Interests: outdoors. Styles: fun.

### Japanese mandoline slicer with a safety guard

Paper-thin onions and even potato slices in a minute flat.

Why this fits: It removes the one slow step that makes weeknight cooking feel long.

Look for: a hand guard that grips small ends and a blade that swaps or adjusts for thickness. Avoid: any slicer sold without a guard; fingers are the price.

Tip: Use the guard for the last third of every vegetable, no exceptions. Dry the blade flat right after washing so it never rusts at the edge.

For: mom, dad, partner, friend, other. Budget: Under $25. Interests: cooking. Styles: practical.

### Enameled cast iron Dutch oven, 4 quart

The pot for Sunday sauce, beans, and bread with a crackling crust.

Why this fits: One heavy pot quietly retires three flimsy ones they keep meaning to replace.

Look for: an even enamel coat with no chips at the rim and a lid that seals with a wobble-free fit. Avoid: thin stamped pots wearing an enamel look.

Tip: First bake: a no-knead loaf, which seasons nothing and proves everything. Wooden or silicone tools only, to keep the enamel unmarked.

For: mom, dad, partner, friend, other. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: cooking. Styles: practical.

### Bread and pasta masterclass for two

An evening class: dough by hand, sauce from scratch, dinner at the end.

Why this fits: They leave with flour on their sleeves and two dishes they will cook for years.

Look for: a class capped small enough that every pair rolls their own dough. Avoid: demonstration-only classes where students only watch.

Tip: Pick a date a few weeks out so anticipation does half the giving. Ask for the recipe cards digitally too; paper ones vanish in a move.

For: partner, mom, dad, friend, other. Budget: $100+. Interests: cooking. Styles: experience.

### Tabletop escape room game box

A locked-room case to crack at the kitchen table, one envelope at a time.

Why this fits: It turns a Friday night into a race they run themselves.

Look for: a case rated for teens and up with a hint system that never needs a phone app. Avoid: one-part boxes that end in under an hour for a group of four.

Tip: Play it with the box top off and snacks outside the evidence zone. The spent case regifts well; sort the envelopes back in order when you finish.

For: kid. Budget: $25-$50. Interests: games. Styles: fun.

### Retro handheld game console with built-in classics

A pocket console loaded with the arcade and 8-bit games they grew up name-dropping.

Why this fits: It starts a tournament in the back seat before anyone asks for the wifi password.

Look for: a bright screen, a battery that lasts a long road trip, and a game list with the real classics. Avoid: consoles whose hundreds of games are the same ten clones.

Tip: Charge it before you wrap it and save a high score under their name. A small hard case keeps it alive in a backpack.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: tech, games. Styles: fun.

### Action camera with a waterproof case

A small tough camera that mounts to a helmet or handlebars and survives the splash zone.

Why this fits: The wipeout reel is the video they will show everyone at dinner.

Look for: waterproof without a separate housing, image stabilization, and mounts in the box. Avoid: no-name cameras whose companion apps vanish from the store.

Tip: Pair it with a small float grip so a dropped camera bobs back up. Charge it before the first ride.

For: kid. Budget: $50-$100. Interests: tech, outdoors. Styles: fun.

Why I built this
The December list
The names were easy.
Each December, I listed Mom, Dad, my in-laws, and my wife, then sat stuck on what to give them.
The store did not help.
Store pages showed the same candles as last year, so I bought a gift card — the gift that says: “I remembered the day. I just do not know you.”
Start with the person.
Five questions ask what they love and what I can spend, then pick from 255 ideas checked by hand. Each pick says why it fits them.
Who made this
Made by a dad, on the side
I'm Billy, a dad in Redmond, Washington. I build these tools on the side, with AI — one idea, one website, no company behind it. The December list above is mine: the stuck names, the gift card, all of it.

How it works
Five questions. Five gift ideas.
You answer.
Five quick questions: who it is for, what they are into, what you can spend.
We search the 255 checked ideas.
Your price range is firm, and no store can pay to rank.
You get five picks.
Best match first. Each pick says why it fits, and your list stays in your browser. When a popular gift is wrong for them, we name it, say why, and leave it out.
Do you link to stores?
Yes, one plain link.
Every idea is a type, not a brand.
Most picks carry a price-check link.
It opens a shopping search for the pick's name.
The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link.
How are the five picks chosen?
Your budget is a hard filter.
Your interests score each idea.
A picked style puts a matching idea first.
Same answers, same order, every time.
Do I need an account?
No. There is no signup and no email. Your saved list lives in your browser only.
Is my list private?
Yes. It is stored on your device and never sent anywhere. Sharing only happens when you tap a share button.
Who made this?
Billy, a dad in Redmond, Washington, built this on the side, with AI. Free, no ads, no accounts. Built with Muse.
What we don't do
We don't sell gifts, and no store can pay to place an idea. Your quiz answers stay in your browser and stay private. The one exception: words on the Ask page are read by an AI helper, then discarded. There is nothing to sign up for, and we ask for no email. Every idea comes from our own hand-checked list of 255, ranked for the person.
Works with your AI
Your AI can run this site's gift picker. Ideas come from the same 255 checked gifts, matched to your person and your budget, not ads.

Common questions
Can a gift under $25 still feel thoughtful?
Yes. Small and useful beats big and random. A meat thermometer, a headlamp, or a book light gets used every week. Pick the one that fits how they spend their days.
Will every idea here cost under $25 in a store?
Stores set real prices, and prices change. Every idea here is in the under $25 budget band in the picker. Check the tag when you buy, and pick another idea here if one runs over.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
Is $25 to $50 enough for a gift that lasts?
Yes. A good pan, a warm scarf, or a strong tool can last for years at this price. Pick the one they will use each week, not the biggest-looking box.
Will every idea here cost $25 to $50 in a store?
Stores set real prices, and prices change. Every idea here is in the $25 to $50 budget band in the picker. Check the tag when you buy, and pick another idea here if one runs over.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
When is a $50 to $100 gift worth it?
When they will use it often and keep it for years. A sharp knife, a weighted blanket, or a parks pass earns its cost. Skip this band if a smaller pick fits them just as well.
Will every idea here cost $50 to $100 in a store?
Stores set real prices, and prices change. Every idea here is in the $50 to $100 budget band in the picker. Check the tag when you buy, and pick another idea here if one runs over.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
When should I spend over $100 on a gift?
Only when you know them well and know they will use it. A mixer, good headphones, or a weekend bag can last for years. If you are not sure, pick a smaller idea and add time with them.
Will every idea here cost over $100 in a store?
Stores set real prices, and prices change. Every idea here is in the $100+ budget band in the picker. Check the tag when you buy, and pick another idea here if one runs far over.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
What are good Christmas gifts for someone who is hard to buy for?
Pick something warm, tasty, or shared. A candle trio makes the house feel ready. A spice subscription keeps giving after Christmas morning. A heated throw gets used all winter.

Any amount here can work. Under $25 covers small, kind picks; $25 to $50 covers most everyday gifts. Spend more only on something they will use or keep for years.

## Page: https://thepresentpicker.com/mcp

The Present Picker gift tools
Tell the assistant who the gift is for. Get gift ideas worth giving.
The picks come from a fixed bank. It holds 255 gift ideas. A person picked each one.
No brands. No exact prices.
The three tools
Pick a gift - up to 5 ideas for one person. They match your budget, likes, and gift kind.
Search gift ideas - up to 10 ideas for one interest. Or search one word, like cooking or coffee. It always says how many fit.
Get gift details - the full story on one idea. Plus 3 ideas like it.
All three are read-only. They buy nothing, book nothing, and collect nothing.
Try these prompts
"I need a gift for my dad. He likes cooking. I can spend $25 to $50."
"What can I get my grandma? Something warm and sweet, under $25."
"Show me gift ideas for a kid who loves science."
"Search your gift ideas for coffee."
"Tell me more about the cast iron skillet idea."
How to add it
Claude: not in the Connectors Directory yet. Not submitted yet, no date promised.
ChatGPT: not in the app directory yet. Not submitted yet, no date promised.
Direct connect: point any MCP client at https://mcp.thepresentpicker.com/mcp . No sign-in, no key.
Good to know
Free. No ads. No accounts.
Ideas are product types, like "a pour-over coffee set". You buy them wherever you like.
Budget is a band, like $25 to $50. Stores set real prices, and prices change.
If only 2 ideas fit your exact ask. The tool says so. It does not pad the list.
Help
Questions or ideas: [email protected]

## Page: https://thepresentpicker.com/privacy

The Present Picker
Privacy
The short version: Your quiz answers stay in your browser. Cloudflare and PostHog count visits here. There are no accounts here.
What the quiz does
You pick a person, interests, and budget.
You may add a first name.
You may add one short description.
The picking math runs in your browser.
Your name and description stay in page memory.
They are never saved or sent.
They clear when you restart the quiz.
The Ask page
One page on this site works in a new way.
That page is the Ask page.
What you type there is read by an AI helper.
The AI helper reads your words.
Then it picks from the same 255 ideas as the quiz.
Nothing you type is saved.
No name is asked.
No contact details are asked.
We count the asks each day, as a plain number.
We count taps on its quiz button too.
Those counts hold no words and no names.
Every other page still runs in your browser.
Your saved list
A list you save stays in your browser.
It holds only gift IDs and person types.
It never reaches us at all.
Tap the remove button to delete one.
Price links
Some picks carry a "See store prices" link.
It opens a shopping search for the pick's name.
The search runs on Bing Shopping.
Prices live at the stores it finds.
The link is a plain search link.
It has no affiliate code and no referral tag.
We earn nothing from the link.
Sharing and prompts
Sharing starts only when you tap Share.
Sharing uses your device share sheet.
Or it copies the text for you.
You choose where the text goes.
The list image is drawn in your browser.
The AI prompt is built in your browser.
You copy it into your own AI.
Site counts
This site loads Cloudflare Web Analytics.
It sends page and performance counts to Cloudflare.
Cloudflare says its beacon uses no cookies.
The home and Ask pages also run PostHog.
PostHog counts page views and quiz starts.
It counts finishes, shares, and return visits.
It counts saved picks, prompts, and images.
PostHog keeps a random ID in your browser.
It tells a first visit from a return visit.
It is not your name or your answers.
Your quiz answers are never sent to it.
It does not record your screen.
AI assistant tools
AI assistant tools are covered separately.
See the tools page for their links.
Children
Adults use this site to buy gifts.
Some gifts here are for children.
It is not directed at children under 13.
Contact
Questions about privacy: [email protected] .
Changes
Changes will appear on this page.
Built with Muse.
More: Home · Terms


## Page: https://thepresentpicker.com/terms

The Present Picker
Terms
The short version: This site gives free gift ideas. Ideas are types, not store listings. You buy wherever you like.
What this site is
These terms cover this website only.
This site is a free gift idea tool.
You answer five short quiz questions.
It returns five gift ideas for you.
Gift lists group the same ideas another way.
There are no ads on this site.
There are no accounts or sign-ups.
The site sells nothing at all.
Where picks come from
Picks come from a fixed bank.
The bank holds 255 gift ideas.
Your budget is a hard filter.
Your interests score each idea.
Your style pick boosts matching ideas.
Same answers always give same picks.
Budget bands are guides, not exact prices.
Stores set real prices, and prices change.
Buying your gift
Some picks carry a price-check link.
It opens a shopping search for the pick's name.
We earn nothing from the link.
It takes no payment from you.
It places no orders for you.
You choose where and what to buy.
Check each idea before you buy.
Accounts and data
The quiz runs in your browser.
Your saved list stays in your browser.
Cloudflare and PostHog count visits here.
PostHog counts quiz starts, finishes, and shares.
See the Privacy page for full details.
No guarantees
This site is provided as is.
We give no warranty of any kind.
We cannot guarantee any gift outcome.
We are not liable for any loss.
Fair use
Use this site only for lawful purposes.
Do not try to break this site.
We may change or stop this site.
Contact
Questions about terms: [email protected] .

Common questions
What is a good gift for a teacher?
Something small and useful they would not buy themselves: a book light for the nightstand stack, good coffee for the morning, a stand that holds a book open at the right angle. Every pick on this page is one of those.
How much should you spend on a teacher gift?
Under $25 is the sweet spot for most class gifts, and the first four picks here sit in that band. A group gift from the whole class can reach for the $50 to $100 picks without any one family spending much.
What should you skip for a teacher?
Skip scented lotions and anything that needs a size or a taste guess. A handwritten note from your child beats both, and it pairs with any pick here.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
What do teens actually want for Christmas?
Things that work with their room, their music, and their friends: a speaker, a game the whole table can play, an instrument they can pick up in minutes. The picks here are built on those three, plus science kits with a real payoff.
How much should you spend on a teen at Christmas?
The $25 to $50 band carries the strongest picks on this page: the speaker, the board game, the star map. Under $25 still lands when the gift starts in the first hour, like the kalimba.
What if the teen is hard to buy for?
Pick the star map of the night they were born. It needs no size, no shade, and no taste guess, and it hangs in their room long after December. Or take the five-question quiz on the home page and narrow the same 255 ideas to five picks for them.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.

Common questions
What is a good gift for a neighbor?
Something small that gets used up or used daily: a candle trio, good olive oil, seeds for spring. It says thanks without asking for shelf space, which is the right size for a neighbor gift.
How much should you spend on a neighbor gift?
Under $25 covers most of the street, and the first four picks here sit in that band. Save the $25 to $50 picks for the neighbor who waters your plants or takes your packages in.
What about a neighbor you barely know?
Stay edible or seasonal: the candle trio and the hot sauce trio need no taste guess beyond sweet or heat. Add a card with your name and house number; that is the part they keep.

Common questions
What is a good $25 to $50 gift for a kid?
A step up from the small picks: a board game the family plays weekly, a building set with real depth, a science kit with more inside. Match the habit and the gift earns its price.
Is the middle band worth it?
It depends on the kid. A clear habit earns the bigger set or the better kit. A kid who loves new things may like a few small picks more. The under $25 page, linked above, holds the small set.
How do I know it will not sit in a closet?
Match the habit, not the holiday. Read the why line on each card: if it sounds like your kid, it will get used.
Do you link to stores or sell these gifts?
Every idea is a type, not a brand. Most picks carry a price-check link that opens a shopping search for the pick's name. The site sells nothing and earns nothing from the link. This site's one job is good ideas.
